title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Ménétrier disease is a rare hypertrophic gastropathy characterized by giant mucosal folds predominantly involving the gastric body and fundus; reduced gastric acid secretion; and protein-losing enteropathy, leading to hypoalbuminemia. The disorder is associated with excessive transforming growth factor α signaling and epidermal growth factor receptor activation, resulting in foveolar hyperplasia and glandular atrophy. In adults, Ménétrier disease typically follows a progressive course and carries an increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma. In children, the condition is usually acute and self-limited and has been linked to cytomegalovirus infection. Helicobacter pylori infection has also been implicated, particularly in adults. Clinical manifestations include epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, peripheral edema, weight loss, and anemia.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Diagnosis is based on endoscopic visualization of enlarged gastric folds, histopathologic confirmation, and exclusion of mimicking conditions. Management focuses on supportive care, treatment of underlying infections when present, acid suppression, nutritional support, and targeted interventions, such as epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor administration, in refractory cases. Complications include severe protein malnutrition and gastric malignancy, with prognosis dependent on age of onset and response to therapy.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Introduction
content: Ménétrier disease is a rare disorder characterized by giant mucosal folds in the proximal stomach, reduced acid secretion, and protein-losing enteropathy with resulting hypoalbuminemia. The distal stomach is typically spared. Alternative terms include "hypoproteinemic hypertrophic gastropathy" and "giant hypertrophic gastritis." [1] The condition predominantly affects men but also occurs in women and children. In adults, Ménétrier disease frequently follows a progressive course and is considered premalignant. The etiopathogenesis is incompletely understood. [2]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Etiology
content: The exact etiology of Ménétrier disease is unclear. The condition is generally considered acquired rather than inherited, although rare familial cases suggest a genetic contribution. A report described a large 4-generation family affected by Ménétrier disease, in which a dominant 1244_1247delACAG alteration in SMAD4 ( a deletion of the adenine–cytosine–adenine–guanine sequence from nucleotide positions 1244 through 1247, resulting in a frameshift mutation), previously linked to juvenile polyposis syndrome, was identified as a likely causative factor. [3] [4]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Etiology
content: A self-limited variant occurs in children and is associated with cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. [5] A similar variant has been reported in adults in association with Helicobacter pylori infection. [6] [7] [8] Overexpression of transforming growth factor α (TGF-α) in the superficial gastric epithelium has been hypothesized to contribute to the pathogenesis of Ménétrier disease in the context of these infections. [9]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Epidemiology
content: The prevalence of Ménétrier disease is unknown, with fewer than 1,000 cases reported to date. The condition affects men more frequently than women. Onset typically occurs in adults aged 30 years or older, with a median age of symptom presentation of 55. Cases in children have also been documented. A study reported 5- and 10-year survival rates of 72.7% and 65%, respectively. Gastric cancer developed in 8.9% of patients after 10 years of follow-up. [10]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Pathophysiology
content: Increased epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling is thought to result from elevated TGF-α production, which promotes proliferation of mucosal epithelial cells. TGF-α, a ligand that activates EGFR, stimulates epithelial cell growth, leading to abundant mucus production. TGF-α reduces acid secretion directly via actions on parietal cells and indirectly via stimulation of somatostatin release. Hypersecretion of mucus impairs absorption of nutrients, electrolytes, and vitamins in the small bowel. Disruption of tight junctions between gastric epithelial cells contributes to malabsorption of essential nutrients, resulting in protein-losing gastropathy. [11] Overexpression of TGF-α also explains hypochlorhydria despite normal or slightly elevated gastric acid levels.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Pathophysiology
content: CMV infection is believed to trigger TGF-α overexpression, thereby activating the EGFR signaling pathway. Excessive TGF-α accumulation in the gastric mucosa may result from viral injury. [12] In Ménétrier disease associated with H pylori , the pathogenesis similarly involves EGFR pathway activation. Overexpression of TGF-α, demonstrated in Ménétrier disease, reproduces the phenotype in transgenic mice. H pylori upregulates the pathway and induces TGF-α overexpression through a mechanism distinct from CMV. [13] The relationship between H pylori infection and the EGFR–TGF-α axis is incompletely understood.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Histopathology
content: The definitive diagnosis of Ménétrier disease requires endoscopic biopsy. Mucosal biopsies may appear nonspecific or normal. However, characteristic histopathologic findings include: Foveolar hyperplasia Oxyntic gland atrophy Reduction in parietal (acid-producing) and chief (pepsinogen-producing) cells Increased eosinophils and plasma cells Edema and smooth muscle hyperplasia in the lamina propria Cystic dilation or corkscrew morphology of epithelial pits Preservation of overall mucosal architecture [14]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Histopathology
content: When mucosal biopsies are nondiagnostic but clinical suspicion for Ménétrier disease remains, deeper gastric biopsies, including the muscularis mucosae, are indicated to identify the findings listed above. [15] Deeper samples may be obtained using jumbo forceps, polypectomy snares, or endoscopic mucosal resection, often eliminating the need for surgical full-thickness biopsies.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- History and Physical
content: Ménétrier disease typically has a subtle onset with progressive manifestations in adults. The most common clinical features include epigastric pain (65%), fatigue (60%), anorexia (45%), weight loss (45%), edema (38%), and vomiting (38%). [16] Additional symptoms include nausea, diarrhea, and gastrointestinal bleeding secondary to gastric erosion or ulcers. [17] Rarely, gastroduodenal intussusception may occur. [18] Clinical features resulting from hypoalbuminemia due to protein-losing enteropathy, such as ascites, pleural effusion, and pericardial effusion, may also be observed.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- History and Physical
content: In children, Ménétrier disease presents acutely and typically resolves spontaneously within several weeks. A history of CMV infection is often reported in pediatric cases, whereas adults may have a history of H pylori infection. [19] Rare associations with other infections, including Mycoplasma pneumoniae , herpes simplex virus, and Giardia lamblia , occur more frequently in children than in adults. A weak association with ulcerative colitis has also been reported. [20]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Evaluation
content: Pierre Ménétrier compared the macroscopic appearance of the pathognomonic thickened gastric mucosa in the disease to cerebral convolutions (gyri). Definitive diagnosis requires endoscopic biopsies, although additional evaluations are often performed before or alongside endoscopy.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Evaluation
content: A barium gastrointestinal series demonstrates marked enlargement of gastric rugal folds along the greater curvature, with excessive mucus secretion diluting barium and impairing mucosal coating. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography shows diffuse gastric mucosal thickening. [21] Rarely, Ménétrier disease presents as gastroduodenal intussusception. [22] Positron emission tomography–computed tomography may reveal increased 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in thickened mucosa due to inflammation, warranting inclusion of Ménétrier disease in the differential diagnosis of abnormal gastric 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose accumulation. [23]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Evaluation
content: Laboratory evaluation should include a complete blood count with differential, complete metabolic panel, ferritin, and gastrin levels. Optional measurements include α1-antitrypsin, fibrinogen, and ceruloplasmin. Assessment for H pylori should be performed using endoscopic biopsy, stool antigen detection, or breath testing. CMV evaluation should include serologic antibody testing and endoscopic biopsies for viral inclusion bodies, with concurrent immunohistochemistry and polymerase chain reaction analysis of biopsy specimens. Typical laboratory findings include hypoalbuminemia (a hallmark), lymphopenia, normal or mildly elevated gastrin, iron deficiency, and reduced levels of α1-antitrypsin, cholesterol, fibrinogen, and ceruloplasmin. [24]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Evaluation
content: Endoscopy reveals giant gastric folds, superficial punctate erosions, and erythema of the proximal gastric mucosa. Endoscopic mucosal or deeper biopsies are required for diagnostic confirmation, as described in the Histopathology section. Patients often exhibit hypochlorhydria with relatively normal serum gastrin. Gastric fluid collection during endoscopy for pH measurement is recommended when available. [25]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Treatment / Management
content: Clinical trials evaluating treatments for Ménétrier disease are limited. Pharmacologic therapies have demonstrated inconsistent efficacy. Supportive treatments include a high-protein diet, proton pump inhibitors, and micronutrient replacement. Albumin infusions may be necessary for patients with significant hypoalbuminemia.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Treatment / Management
content: Treatment of H pylori and CMV infections is indicated when tests are positive. Eradication of H pylori has been shown to improve disease in some patients. Similarly, ganciclovir therapy is effective in certain cases associated with CMV. [26]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Treatment / Management
content: Octreotide, a somatostatin analog, has demonstrated benefit in case reports. The agent modulates the TGF-α–EGFR signaling pathway underlying the pathogenic mechanism. Reported dosing ranges from 100 to 600 µg daily, subcutaneously or intravenously, or 10 to 60 mg intramuscularly every 4 weeks using the depot formulation. [27]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Treatment / Management
content: Cetuximab was evaluated in a small phase I, single-arm, open-label case series in patients with severe Ménétrier disease treated for 1 month. Treatment produced significant improvement in quality of life and biochemical parameters. Cetuximab, a recombinant monoclonal antibody of the immunoglobulin G1 subclass, binds the extracellular portion of EGFR, thereby inhibiting TGF-α binding. To date, this single clinical trial represents the only formal evaluation of pharmacologic therapy in Ménétrier disease. Dosing consists of an initial loading dose of intravenous cetuximab (400 mg/m² body surface area), followed by 3 weekly intravenous infusions of 250 mg/m² for 12 months. [28]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Treatment / Management
content: Surgery is indicated in refractory cases with disease progression accompanied by severe abdominal pain, weight loss, bleeding, or pyloric obstruction. Partial or total gastrectomy is a valid option for patients with persistent, debilitating symptoms or increased risk of gastric cancer. Total gastrectomy is preferred over partial resection due to superior surgical outcomes. [29]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is caused by gastrinomas that secrete gastrin ectopically. Approximately 80% to 90% of these tumors are located in the “gastrinoma triangle,” which includes the 1st and 2nd portions of the duodenum, the head and neck of the pancreas, and the bile duct distal to the cystic duct takeoff. Excessive gastric acid secretion results in refractory acid reflux and peptic ulcers in the postbulbar duodenum and jejunum. Histopathologic examination demonstrates parietal cell hyperplasia.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Differential Diagnosis
content: H pylori gastritis presents with gastritis, duodenitis, gastric ulcers, or duodenal ulcers without other findings characteristic of Ménétrier disease, and testing for H pylori is positive. Hypertrophic lymphocytic gastritis closely resembles Ménétrier disease but is distinguished histologically by severe inflammation with a predominant intraepithelial lymphocytic infiltrate. Hypertrophic hypersecretory gastropathy involves hypersecretion from all glandular cell types of the stomach, including acid, pepsin, and mucin, with histologic evidence of foveolar and oxyntic gland hyperplasia. [30]

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Gastric polyps are typically more focal, may be numerous, and can mimic Ménétrier disease. Gastric adenocarcinoma is differentiated pathologically by dysplasia, malignant features, and architectural loss. Gastric lymphoma is identified through biopsy. Infectious etiologies, including histoplasmosis, syphilis, and tuberculosis, and infiltrative disorders such as sarcoidosis, should also be considered in the differential diagnosis.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Prognosis
content: In children, Ménétrier disease is typically associated with CMV infection and is self-limited. Resolution occurs spontaneously over a period ranging from several weeks to months. Symptomatic improvement has been reported following CMV treatment with ganciclovir. [31] In adults, the disease generally follows a progressive course. Symptom resolution has been observed in a limited number of adult cases after eradication of H pylori . Patients with Ménétrier disease carry an increased risk of malignancy, primarily gastric carcinoma and gastric lymphoma. Endoscopic surveillance is recommended by some experts for early detection of dysplasia or carcinoma.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Complications
content: In adults, Ménétrier disease follows a progressive course and may be associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Complications commonly include malignant transformation, thromboembolic events, and gastric outlet obstruction. Surgical resection of the stomach carries additional risks, including anastomotic leak, fistula formation, and hemorrhage.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Consultations
content: Referral to a gastroenterologist or surgical endoscopist is required to obtain biopsies for definitive diagnosis of Ménétrier disease, manage symptoms, and conduct ongoing endoscopic surveillance due to the risk of gastric cancer. Surgical consultation is indicated for patients with refractory symptoms when gastrectomy is under consideration or planned. A dietitian should provide guidance on implementing a high-protein diet.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Deterrence of complications in Ménétrier disease emphasizes early recognition, timely referral, and proactive management to prevent progressive protein loss, malnutrition, and potential malignant transformation. Primary care clinicians and gastroenterologists are central in monitoring at-risk patients, identifying infectious triggers such as CMV and H pylori , and initiating appropriate eradication or antiviral therapy when indicated. Supportive interventions, including implementation of a high-protein diet, micronutrient replacement, and albumin supplementation, reduce the risk of hypoalbuminemia-related complications. Pharmacologic therapy or surgical intervention may be employed in refractory cases.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education is critical to optimize outcomes and engagement in care. Clinicians should inform patients and families about the nature of the disease, common symptoms such as fatigue, epigastric pain, and edema, and the importance of adherence to nutritional and pharmacologic regimens, including a high-protein diet. Education should also emphasize regular endoscopic surveillance, infection management, and prompt reporting of new or worsening symptoms. Equipping patients with knowledge about their condition supports self-care, enhances safety, and facilitates collaboration with the interprofessional healthcare team.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Ménétrier disease is a rare gastric disorder characterized by giant mucosal folds, hypochlorhydria, and protein-losing enteropathy, frequently resulting in hypoalbuminemia. The disease follows a progressive course in adults and is self-limited in children, with potential triggers including CMV and H pylori infections. Diagnosis requires endoscopic evaluation with targeted biopsies and laboratory assessment. Management is multifaceted, encompassing infection eradication, pharmacologic therapy, supportive care, and surgical intervention in refractory cases. Primary care clinicians are essential for early recognition and referral to gastroenterology for surveillance and comprehensive evaluation.

title: Ménétrier Disease  -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective management relies on interprofessional collaboration. Physicians, gastroenterologists, and advanced practitioners coordinate diagnostic and therapeutic decisions, while nurses and pharmacists ensure monitoring and medication management. Dietitians provide nutritional support to mitigate protein loss, and pathologists contribute critical histologic interpretation. Open communication, accurate documentation, and shared decision-making enhance patient-centered care, optimize outcomes, and maintain safety throughout the continuum of care.
